The descriptive-parsimony tension arises because nature's complexity often resists simple explanation, yet understanding requires compression. A model that captures every observational nuance becomes unwieldy and overfits, predicting noise rather than signal. A maximally parsimonious model risks being so austere it misses essential mechanisms, predicting poorly despite elegant form.

This trade-off likely cannot be definitively resolved because "best" depends on context and purpose. Prediction often favors different complexity levels than explanation does. Occam's razor is methodological heuristic, not metaphysical truthâ€”nature need not privilege simplicity. The bias-variance decomposition in statistics formalizes this: simpler models have low variance but potentially high bias; complex models fit training data closely but may generalize poorly.

Practical science navigates this through model selection criteria that penalize complexity (AIC, BIC) and cross-validation testing. The "right" balance shifts with data quality, domain maturity, and investigative goals. Phenomenological models in fluid dynamics embrace descriptive complexity because fundamental derivation from molecular principles remains intractable. Particle physics pursues unification and parsimony because empirical success of simple symmetry principles has been extraordinary.

What changes historically is our judgment of which complexities are artificial scaffolding versus which reflect genuine natural structure. Ptolemaic epicycles seemed necessary descriptive apparatus until Kepler and Newton revealed them as artifacts of the wrong framework. But no meta-principle guarantees this resolution universally. Some domains may be irreducibly complex; others await their Kepler. The tension is intrinsic to modeling itselfâ€”the map-territory distinction ensures perfect fidelity requires abandoning the compression that makes models useful.

What are the fundamental tensions between descriptive accuracy and theoretical parsimony in scientific model-building, and can this trade-off ever be definitively resolved?
Claude
📋
The descriptive-parsimony tension arises because nature's complexity often resists simple explanation, yet understanding requires compression. A model that captures every observational nuance becomes unwieldy and overfits, predicting noise rather than signal. A maximally parsimonious model risks being so austere it misses essential mechanisms, predicting poorly despite elegant form.

This trade-off likely cannot be definitively resolved because "best" depends on context and purpose. Prediction often favors different complexity levels than explanation does. Occam's razor is methodological heuristic, not metaphysical truth—nature need not privilege simplicity. The bias-variance decomposition in statistics formalizes this: simpler models have low variance but potentially high bias; complex models fit training data closely but may generalize poorly.

Practical science navigates this through model selection criteria that penalize complexity (AIC, BIC) and cross-validation testing. The "right" balance shifts with data quality, domain maturity, and investigative goals. Phenomenological models in fluid dynamics embrace descriptive complexity because fundamental derivation from molecular principles remains intractable. Particle physics pursues unification and parsimony because empirical success of simple symmetry principles has been extraordinary.

What changes historically is our judgment of which complexities are artificial scaffolding versus which reflect genuine natural structure. Ptolemaic epicycles seemed necessary descriptive apparatus until Kepler and Newton revealed them as artifacts of the wrong framework. But no meta-principle guarantees this resolution universally. Some domains may be irreducibly complex; others await their Kepler. The tension is intrinsic to modeling itself—the map-territory distinction ensures perfect fidelity requires abandoning the compression that makes models useful.📄 View as Document
